newsitem.title: SOUTH KOREA: S.Korean telecom operators post '96 net gains.
newsitem.headline: S.Korean telecom operators post '96 net gains.

text.p: South Korea's two listed telecommunications service providers saw a rise in earnings in calendar 1996, but analysts said on Friday the gains were smaller than had been expected.

While increased competition ate into Dacom Corp's growth, Korea Mobile Telecom Corp used increased depreciation and other costs to tone down an otherwise strong showing, said Hannuri-Salomon Securities analyst Jon Chong-hwa.
"Korea Mobile Telecom made a lot of effort to depress its profit," Jon said. "It was afraid that too-strong a showing would invite higher tariffs."

Korea Mobile, the nation's largest mobile telecommunications service provider, reported net profit of 195.5 billion won ($226 million) last year, on sales of 2.68 trillion. This compared to 180.8 billion won profit on revenue of 1.32 trillion in 1995.
Earnings per share (EPS) in 1996 were 33,804 won versus 31,809 won in 1995.
Analysts said they had earlier forecast net profits between 300 billion to 400 billion won for 1996.

Dacom, South Korea's second long-distance telephone operator, posted a net income of 15.2 billion won in 1996 on sales of 620.8 billion against 13.4 billion in earnings on turnover of 369.8 billion in 1995.
Dacom's 1996 EPS was 1,104 won, against 1,073 the year earlier.
The company had earlier predicted it would see net earnings of more than 20 billion won, according to analysts.
Korea Mobile said in a statement that its sales growth was due primarily to strong increases in both cellular and paging subscribers.
Cellular revenue amounted to 1.57 trillion won, 59 percent of its total revenue. This was an 85 percent increase over 1995, due in part to a sharp jump in cellular subscribers.
Paging revenue reached 587.3 billion won and accounted for 22 percent of the company's sales.

Korea Mobile launched code division multiple access (CDMA) cellular services last year. As of December 31, 1996, the company said it had a 67 percent share of the Korean CDMA market, with 592,272 subscribers.
CDMA is a digital technology format for data transmission by cellular phones and is in commercial service only in a few regions, including South Korea, the United States and Hong Kong.
Increased competition in the telecommunications service industry slowed Dacom's earnings, analysts said.

Dacom launched its domestic long distance service last year, but did not win as large a market share as it had expected, analysts said. They estimated the company had about a 10 percent share, compared to its prediction of 15 percent.
Dacom officials were not available for comment.
